<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_section"><a href="#S5" title="In RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">5 </span>Related Work</span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_section">

<article class="ltx_document">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory 
<br class="ltx_break">for Robot Learning</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Synthetic data generated by video generative models has shown promise for robot learning as a scalable pipeline, but it often suffers from inconsistent action quality due to imperfectly generated videos. Recently, vision-language models (VLMs) have been leveraged to validate video quality, but they have limitations in distinguishing physically accurate videos and, even then, cannot directly evaluate the generated actions themselves. To tackle this issue, we introduce RoboCurate, a novel synthetic robot data generation framework that evaluates and filters the quality of annotated actions by comparing them with simulation replay. Specifically, RoboCurate replays the predicted actions in a simulator and assesses action quality by measuring the consistency of motion between the simulator rollout and the generated video. In addition, we unlock observation diversity beyond the available dataset via image-to-image editing and apply action-preserving video-to-video transfer to further augment appearance. We observe RoboCurate’s generated data yield substantial relative improvements in success rates compared to using real data only, achieving +70.1% on GR-1 Tabletop (300 demos), +16.1% on DexMimicGen in the pre-training setup, and +179.9% in the challenging real-world ALLEX humanoid dexterous manipulation setting.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Machine Learning, ICML
</div><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_affiliationnotice"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">affiliationnotice: </span>Equal contribution</span></span></span>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18742v1/robocurate_figure.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/393;" width="476" height="393" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Overview of RoboCurate<span id="S1.F1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">. (1) We generate diverse neural trajectory by applying image-to-image (I2I) model for scene diversity and video-to-video (V2V) model for appearance diversity, respectively. (2) We then filter neural trajectory using simulator-replay consistency, retaining only those for which a classifier predicts the motion in the generated video matches the simulator rollout.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Robot foundation models (RFMs; <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zitkovich et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bjorck et al., 2025</a>)</cite>) have achieved strong performance across diverse robotics domains, <span id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e</span>.<span id="S1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">g</span>., manipulation, locomotion, and navigation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hirose et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. The key component of this success is large-scale robotics datasets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">O’Neill et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> spanning diverse tasks and embodiments, often leveraging foundation models like vision-language models (VLMs) and video generative models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cheang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shen et al., 2025</a>)</cite> for action generation by bridging world knowledge and commonsense with robotic actions. This serves as a form of pre-training for action data, enabling RFMs to adapt to downstream tasks with little or no task-specific fine-tuning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Despite its success, robotics data remains far more limited than vision and language data due to costly and labor-intensive collection processes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Khazatsky et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Walke et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, which fundamentally constrain large-scale pre-training.
To address this problem, prior research has focused on simulation-based synthetic data as a substitute for real data, but simulation suffers from visual discrepancies with real-world environments, limited knowledge transfer to real-world settings (<span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i</span>.<span id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e</span>., sim-to-real gap), and requires substantial engineering effort to generate diverse environments and action data. Meanwhile, neural trajectory, <span id="S1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i</span>.<span id="S1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e</span>., synthetic data generated by video generative models, have emerged as a promising alternative, as they are visually similar to real-world data than simulation. Moreover, those models can generate diverse task videos conditioned on text prompts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. This approach annotates episodes by mapping videos to actions through inverse dynamics models (IDMs) trained on real data. Several studies have experimentally shown that neural trajectory can improve generalization and enable learning novel actions beyond the training dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">However, neural trajectory pipelines often face quality issues. Unlike in simulation, the video generation stage can fail to follow input instructions or produce physically implausible videos (<span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e</span>.<span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">g</span>., objects overlapping or deforming unnaturally), which leads to incorrect action annotations. Moreover, even when videos are accurate, relying on learned models such as IDMs instead of ground-truth annotators can produce low-quality action labels, degrading overall data quality and ultimately leading to suboptimal downstream policy performance.
To address this problem, recent work has employed VLMs to judge instruction following or video plausibility <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Motamed et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bansal et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
However, such judgments are typically too coarse to capture task-critical motion for policy learning (<span id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e</span>.<span id="S1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">g</span>., whether the arm moves far enough to reach the object) and often stop at superficial compliance with basic physics without directly evaluating the actions themselves. This highlights the necessity for a new method that can verify actions with visual correspondence and physical grounding.</p>
</div>
<section id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Contributions.</h4>

<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To overcome this limitation, we propose RoboCurate, a unified framework that (1) generates synthetic robot data and (2) filters neural trajectory by quality via simulator-replay consistency, while supporting diverse scene and task generation. The core idea is to leverage a simulator to replay the generated action sequences, producing proxy robot videos with guaranteed correspondence to the generated actions. By measuring visual motion consistency between these simulator-replayed videos and the synthesized videos, we can evaluate both the visual quality of the generated data and the correctness of action labels. Concretely, we replay IDM-predicted actions in a simulator to render a rollout video, and reformulate alignment as motion matching between the generated video and the simulator replay. To assess this match, we train a lightweight attentive probe on top of a pre-trained video encoder to classify whether a video pair exhibits consistent motion patterns and robot geometry.
In addition, we introduce a controllable visual diversification pipeline that expands initial scenes and augments generated videos using recent diffusion models.
Specifically, we employ (1) image-to-image (I2I) editing to substantially increase scene diversity, and (2) action-preserving video-to-video (V2V) transfer to augment appearance while preserving motion dynamics. Together, such pipeline generates high-quality data that reflects a wide range of realistic environmental variations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We verify the effectiveness of RoboCurate across diverse scenarios. We pre-train vision-language-action models (VLAs) on Fourier ActionNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fourier ActionNet Team, 2025</a>)</cite> and evaluate on GR-1 Tabletop <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">NVIDIA et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and DexMimicGen <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> benchmarks. We further perform co-finetuning with real-robot evaluation on the ALLEX humanoid. In the pre-training setup, RoboCurate yields remarkable relative gains compared to real-data-only baseline, achieving a +70.1% on GR-1 Tabletop (300 demos) and a +16.1% on DexMimicGen. In contrast, the base synthetic data generation framework <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> yields only marginal gains over the same real-data-only baseline of +26.6% and +4.0% on the same benchmarks, respectively.
We observe that this trend generalizes to the real ALLEX humanoid in the co-finetuning setup: RoboCurate demonstrates a +179.9% relative improvement in success rate, whereas <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al. (2025)</a></cite> achieves a +100.0% gain. Notably, RoboCurate further demonstrates strong out-of-distribution generalization on the challenging real-world ALLEX humanoid dexterous manipulation environment, achieving a +162.3% relative improvement on novel object pick-and-place tasks and enabling emergent success on novel action tasks (from 0.0% to 25.0%).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Preliminaries</h2>

<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Video diffusion models.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent video generative models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Blattmann et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kong et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wan et al., 2025</a>)</cite> typically operate in a compressed latent space to reduce computational complexity. Given a video <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐰</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{w}</annotation></semantics></math> in pixel space, an encoder <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}</annotation></semantics></math> maps it to a latent representation <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}=\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{w})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐰</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}=\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{w})</annotation></semantics></math>. To learn the video distribution within this space, we employ the Flow Matching (FM) framework <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lipman et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, which defines a probability path <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> linearly interpolating between the data <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math> and Gaussian noise <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\epsilon}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\epsilon}</annotation></semantics></math>, with timestep <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S2.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{t}=(1-t)\mathbf{x}+t\boldsymbol{\epsilon}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐱</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{t}=(1-t)\mathbf{x}+t\boldsymbol{\epsilon}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">The diffusion model performs as a velocity predictor <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>, trained to regress the target velocity field <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}=\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐱</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}=\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math>. This is achieved by minimizing the mean squared error (MSE) objective:</p>
<table id="S2.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t,\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\mathbf{c}}\left[\|v_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,\mathbf{c})-(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\mathbf{x})\|^{2}_{2}\right]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐜</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐜</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐱</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t,\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\mathbf{c}}\left[\|v_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,\mathbf{c})-(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\mathbf{x})\|^{2}_{2}\right],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{c}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes conditioning information.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Inverse dynamics models.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Inverse dynamics models (IDMs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Baker et al., 2022</a>)</cite> predict actions between a current observation <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and a future observation <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t+H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t+H}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the action horizon. Formally, IDMs estimate the intermediate action sequence as <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="a_{t:t+H-1}=\mathrm{IDM}(x_{t},x_{t+H})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>IDM</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t:t+H-1}=\mathrm{IDM}(x_{t},x_{t+H})</annotation></semantics></math>.
We use Diffusion Transformer (DiT) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peebles and Xie, 2023</a>)</cite> as our inverse dynamics model, trained with a flow-matching objective. At inference time, the model denoises the entire action sequence <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="a_{t:t+H-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t:t+H-1}</annotation></semantics></math> conditioned on the input frames.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As a result, IDMs serve as a pseudo-action labeler that converts action-free video into action-labeled trajectory. Concretely, using a pre-trained image-to-video (I2V) diffusion model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wan et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ali et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, we generate a synthetic task-execution video from an initial frame and a task instruction. We then apply IDMs to current and future frame pairs along the video to infer actions. This yields neural trajectory, consisting of paired synthetic videos and pseudo-labeled action sequences, enabling policy training on action-free data.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Imitation learning for policy training.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our goal is to learn a policy <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> for robot manipulation from demonstration data. We follow an imitation learning (IL) framework, where the policy predicts actions conditioned on observations and proprioceptive states. We assume access to a limited real-world dataset <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{real}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>real</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{real}}</annotation></semantics></math> and neural trajectory <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{syn}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>syn</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{syn}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and train the policy on the combined dataset
<math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{D}_{\text{real}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\text{syn}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>real</mtext></msub><mo>∪</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>syn</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{D}_{\text{real}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\text{syn}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Specifically, given observation <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, task instruction <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>I</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I</annotation></semantics></math>, and proprioceptive state <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, the policy outputs an action chunk <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="A_{t}=a_{t:t+H-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{t}=a_{t:t+H-1}</annotation></semantics></math>. In our experiments, we use VLA with diffusion-based action head as the base policy, and optimize it with the following flow-matching objective:</p>
<table id="S2.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{IL}}(\theta;\mathcal{D})=\mathbb{E}_{t,A_{t},\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\tau}\Big[\big\|v_{\theta}(A_{t}^{\tau},\tau\mid o_{t},q_{t},I)-(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-A_{t})\big\|_{2}^{2}\Big]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>IL</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>;</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">[</mo><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="1.200em" rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>τ</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msubsup><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="1.200em" rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{IL}}(\theta;\mathcal{D})=\mathbb{E}_{t,A_{t},\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\tau}\Big[\big\|v_{\theta}(A_{t}^{\tau},\tau\mid o_{t},q_{t},I)-(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-A_{t})\big\|_{2}^{2}\Big],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>𝟎</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐈</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})</annotation></semantics></math>, and
<math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{t}^{\tau}=\tau A_{t}+(1-\tau)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>τ</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{t}^{\tau}=\tau A_{t}+(1-\tau)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We note that <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{syn}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>syn</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{syn}}</annotation></semantics></math> has zero-padded proprioceptive states, since IDMs do not predict state information.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Method</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present RoboCurate, a novel neural trajectory generation framework that increases diversity via controllable video generation and filters low-quality samples by evaluating motion similarity between generated video and simulator replay. In Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Generating Plausible Manipulation Scenarios ‣ 3 Method ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>, we introduce our video-level neural trajectory generation stage and the approaches to promote diversity. In Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Action-level Filtering of Neural Trajectory ‣ 3 Method ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>, we propose a filtering strategy that verifies IDM-predicted actions by checking their consistency with the generated video through simulator rollout. In Section <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Improve Neural Trajectory via Best-of-N Sampling ‣ 3 Method ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>, we show that our filtering strategy can also be applied directly during generation stage via Best-of-N sampling. We provide overview of RoboCurate in Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Generating Plausible Manipulation Scenarios</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To generate diverse robot synthetic videos using a video generative model, we control two factors: scene visuals and task instructions. For scene visuals, we inject visual variance with two components: (1) image-to-image (I2I) editing on the initial frame for scene-level variation, and (2) video-to-video (V2V) transfer for appearance diversity while preserving initial motion. For task instructions, we use VLM to identify plausible novel instructions for a given initial scene, and condition video generation on each generated task instruction. We detail each diversification factor below.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Expanding visual diversity.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We perform instruction-guided image editing to generate diverse observations while preserving the underlying manipulation setup. Since the edited image should remain a valid starting state for video generative model (<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e</span>.<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">g</span>., target object and placement should remain physically plausible), we additionally employ a Canny edge map as a condition to preserve original scene structure. We then carefully design systematic prompts to induce controlled visual variations. Specifically, we first query VLM to produce a detailed description of the initial image, and combine it with the original task instruction to identify the target object and relevant manipulation context. Using these as context, we generate multiple edited variants along four axes: (1) table appearance, (2) target object identity and appearance, (3) lighting, and (4) background. Finally, we feed each edited initial frame into an image-to-video diffusion model with plausible task scenarios. We provide additional prompt details for image editing in Appendix <a href="#A3.SS3" title="C.3 System Prompts for Image-to-Image Editing ‣ Appendix C Prompt for VLM ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">While I2I editing can substantially expand visual diversity at the image level, we further augment diversity at the video level. Specifically, we apply video-to-video (V2V) transfer to successful synthetic videos to diversify their appearance while preserving motion dynamics. Since the transferred video typically retains the robot motion, we reuse the action annotations labeled by IDMs. Concretely, we condition V2V transfer on Canny edge videos to preserve the original video structure, and use system prompts analogous to our image editing pipeline along the same four axes. To ensure action reuse remains valid, we keep object identity and shape unchanged and only modify texture and color. We additionally prepend an instruction to maintain the robot’s color, as the embodiment should remain unchanged. See Appendix <a href="#A3.SS4" title="C.4 System Prompts for Video-to-Video Transfer ‣ Appendix C Prompt for VLM ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.4</span></a> for V2V transfer prompt details.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18742v1/attn_probe_figure.png" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:210/133;" width="210" height="133" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S3.F3.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
<span id="S3.F3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Examples of negative pairs for attentive probe training.</span> We construct negative pairs from real-world dataset by inducing temporal shifts or sampling video from different episodes.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Expanding task instructions.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We generate synthetic robot videos conditioned on an initial frame and a language instruction. For effective policy learning, it is crucial that the videos contain meaningful robot-object interactions. To achieve this, we use a proprietary VLM to generate plausible task instructions conditioned on the initial frame. Since naive VLM querying may produce wrong instruction templates or physically infeasible robot actions, we employ few-shot prompting with examples from the original dataset to ensure consistency. Overall, we design novel task instructions along four axes: (1) behavior, (2) target object, (3) placement, and (4) robot hand type. We explicitly specify the active hand to maintain a 1:1 ratio, since we consider bimanual manipulation in downstream tasks. We provide additional prompt details for task instruction generation in Appendix <a href="#A3.SS1" title="C.1 Task Instruction for Image-to-Video Generative Model ‣ Appendix C Prompt for VLM ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Action-level Filtering of Neural Trajectory</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While we can generate diverse neural trajectory by expanding scene visuals and task instructions, they can still contain noisy action labels: physically implausible video motion or IDM prediction errors can make the predicted action inconsistent with the video. To ensure the quality of the training data, it is necessary to identify and filter out such invalid samples. Specifically, we represent each neural-trajectory sample as a generated video paired with an IDM-predicted action, <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathbf{w}_{\text{gen}},a_{\texttt{IDM}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mtext>gen</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">IDM</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathbf{w}_{\text{gen}},a_{\texttt{IDM}})</annotation></semantics></math>. To validate <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{\texttt{IDM}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">IDM</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{\texttt{IDM}}</annotation></semantics></math>, RoboCurate replays <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{\texttt{IDM}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">IDM</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{\texttt{IDM}}</annotation></semantics></math> in simulator and renders the corresponding rollout video <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{w}_{\text{sim}}(a_{\texttt{IDM}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mtext>sim</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">IDM</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{w}_{\text{sim}}(a_{\texttt{IDM}})</annotation></semantics></math>, whose robot motion is consistent with <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{\texttt{IDM}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">IDM</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{\texttt{IDM}}</annotation></semantics></math>. This converts the action verification problem into a motion-consistency comparison between two videos, <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathbf{w}_{\text{gen}},\mathbf{w}_{\text{sim}}(a_{\texttt{IDM}}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mtext>gen</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mtext>sim</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">IDM</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathbf{w}_{\text{gen}},\mathbf{w}_{\text{sim}}(a_{\texttt{IDM}}))</annotation></semantics></math>. To solve this motion-consistency comparison problem, we propose an an attentive probe on top of a frozen video encoder.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">First, we carefully construct positive and negative pairs (see Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ Expanding visual diversity. ‣ 3.1 Generating Plausible Manipulation Scenarios ‣ 3 Method ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>) from real-world demonstrations <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{T}=\{(\mathbf{w}_{\text{real}},a_{\text{real}})\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mtext>real</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mtext>real</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{T}=\{(\mathbf{w}_{\text{real}},a_{\text{real}})\}</annotation></semantics></math> to train the probe to detect subtle motion mismatches. Since neural trajectory can contain noisy action labels and may mislead supervision, we do not use them to train our attentive probe. Concretely, for each real action <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{\text{real}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mtext>real</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{\text{real}}</annotation></semantics></math>, we render a simulator rollout video
<math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{w}_{\text{sim}}(a_{\text{real}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mtext>sim</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mtext>real</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{w}_{\text{sim}}(a_{\text{real}})</annotation></semantics></math> and build positive (aligned) pairs:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{P}^{+}=\Big\{\big(\mathbf{w}_{\text{real}}^{t:t+H},\ \mathbf{w}_{\text{sim}}(a_{\text{real}})^{t:t+H}\big)\Big\}_{t}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐰</mi><mtext>real</mtext><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></mrow></msubsup><mo rspace="0.667em">,</mo><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mtext>sim</mtext></msub><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mtext>real</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{P}^{+}=\Big\{\big(\mathbf{w}_{\text{real}}^{t:t+H},\ \mathbf{w}_{\text{sim}}(a_{\text{real}})^{t:t+H}\big)\Big\}_{t},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> is the starting time of video clip and <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> is fixed clip length. We also design negative pairs <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{P}^{-}=\mathcal{P}^{-}_{\text{shift}}\cup\mathcal{P}^{-}_{\text{cross}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mtext>shift</mtext><mo>−</mo></msubsup><mo>∪</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mtext>cross</mtext><mo>−</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{P}^{-}=\mathcal{P}^{-}_{\text{shift}}\cup\mathcal{P}^{-}_{\text{cross}}</annotation></semantics></math> of two types:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">(1) <span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Temporally shifted negatives.</span> These negatives deliberately misalign time within the same episode:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{P}^{-}_{\text{shift}}=\Big\{\big(\mathbf{w}_{\text{real}}^{t:t+H},\ \mathbf{w}_{\text{sim}}(a_{\text{real}})^{t^{\prime}:t^{\prime}+H}\big)\ \big|\ t^{\prime}\neq t\Big\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mtext>shift</mtext><mo>−</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐰</mi><mtext>real</mtext><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></mrow></msubsup><mo rspace="0.667em">,</mo><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mtext>sim</mtext></msub><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mtext>real</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" rspace="0.500em">)</mo></mrow><mo fence="false" maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" rspace="0.667em" stretchy="true">|</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>≠</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{P}^{-}_{\text{shift}}=\Big\{\big(\mathbf{w}_{\text{real}}^{t:t+H},\ \mathbf{w}_{\text{sim}}(a_{\text{real}})^{t^{\prime}:t^{\prime}+H}\big)\ \big|\ t^{\prime}\neq t\Big\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">(2) <span id="S3.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cross-episode negatives.</span> These negatives pair a real clip with a simulator rollout from a different episode:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{P}^{-}_{\text{cross}}=\Big\{\big(\mathbf{w}_{\text{real}}^{t:t+H},\ \mathbf{w}_{\text{sim}}({a}^{\prime}_{\text{real}})^{t:t+H}\big)\ \big|\ a^{\prime}_{\text{real}}\neq a_{\text{real}}\Big\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mtext>cross</mtext><mo>−</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐰</mi><mtext>real</mtext><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></mrow></msubsup><mo rspace="0.667em">,</mo><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mtext>sim</mtext></msub><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mtext>real</mtext><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" rspace="0.500em">)</mo></mrow><mo fence="false" maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" rspace="0.667em" stretchy="true">|</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mtext>real</mtext><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>≠</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mtext>real</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{P}^{-}_{\text{cross}}=\Big\{\big(\mathbf{w}_{\text{real}}^{t:t+H},\ \mathbf{w}_{\text{sim}}({a}^{\prime}_{\text{real}})^{t:t+H}\big)\ \big|\ a^{\prime}_{\text{real}}\neq a_{\text{real}}\Big\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}^{+}\cup\mathcal{P}^{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>∪</mo><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}^{+}\cup\mathcal{P}^{-}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the training dataset for the attentive probe. For a sampled pair <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="(\mathbf{w}_{1}^{t_{1}:t_{1}+H},\mathbf{w}_{2}^{t_{2}:t_{2}+H})\sim\mathcal{P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐰</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐰</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∼</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathbf{w}_{1}^{t_{1}:t_{1}+H},\mathbf{w}_{2}^{t_{2}:t_{2}+H})\sim\mathcal{P}</annotation></semantics></math>,
we encode each clip using a pre-trained video encoder <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathbf{z}_{1}=f_{\phi}(\mathbf{w}_{1}^{t_{1}:t_{1}+H}),\quad\mathbf{z}_{2}=f_{\phi}(\mathbf{w}_{2}^{t_{2}:t_{2}+H})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐳</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐰</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><msub><mi>𝐳</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐰</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{z}_{1}=f_{\phi}(\mathbf{w}_{1}^{t_{1}:t_{1}+H}),\quad\mathbf{z}_{2}=f_{\phi}(\mathbf{w}_{2}^{t_{2}:t_{2}+H}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Next, we concatenate the embeddings and feed them to an attention-based probe <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{\theta}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{\theta}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> to predict alignment. The attentive probe consists of a single cross-attention layer with a learnable query token that attends to the concatenated video embeddings, followed by a linear head that outputs an alignment logit <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell=g_{\theta}\!\left([\mathbf{z}_{1},\mathbf{z}_{2}]\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐳</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐳</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell=g_{\theta}\!\left([\mathbf{z}_{1},\mathbf{z}_{2}]\right)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we train <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> using binary cross-entropy loss.
Let the alignment probability <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=\sigma(\ell)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=\sigma(\ell)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the sigmoid function. The training objective is</p>
<table id="S3.Ex8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(\theta;\mathcal{P})=\mathbb{E}_{((\mathbf{w}_{1},\mathbf{w}_{2}),y)\sim\mathcal{P}}\Bigl[-y\log p-(1-y)\log(1-p)\Bigr]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.800em">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.800em">θ</mi><mo mathsize="0.800em">,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.800em">𝒫</mi><mo maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.800em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.800em">𝔼</mi><mrow><mrow><mo maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">(</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.800em">𝐰</mi><mn mathsize="0.800em">1</mn></msub><mo mathsize="0.800em">,</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.800em">𝐰</mi><mn mathsize="0.800em">2</mn></msub><mo maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">)</mo></mrow><mo mathsize="0.800em">,</mo><mi mathsize="0.800em">y</mi><mo maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">)</mo></mrow><mo mathsize="0.800em">∼</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.800em">𝒫</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo mathsize="0.800em">−</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.800em">y</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.800em">log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi mathsize="0.800em">p</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.800em">−</mo><mrow><mrow><mo maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">(</mo><mrow><mn mathsize="0.800em">1</mn><mo mathsize="0.800em">−</mo><mi mathsize="0.800em">y</mi></mrow><mo maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.800em">log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">(</mo><mrow><mn mathsize="0.800em">1</mn><mo mathsize="0.800em">−</mo><mi mathsize="0.800em">p</mi></mrow><mo maxsize="0.800em" minsize="0.800em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="0.800em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(\theta;\mathcal{P})=\mathbb{E}_{((\mathbf{w}_{1},\mathbf{w}_{2}),y)\sim\mathcal{P}}\Bigl[-y\log p-(1-y)\log(1-p)\Bigr].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p7.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=1</annotation></semantics></math> only if <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\big(\mathbf{w}_{1},\mathbf{w}_{2})\in\mathcal{P}^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\big(\mathbf{w}_{1},\mathbf{w}_{2})\in\mathcal{P}^{+}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=0</annotation></semantics></math> otherwise. At inference time, given a neural trajectory sample <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathbf{w}_{\text{gen}},a_{\texttt{IDM}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mtext>gen</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">IDM</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathbf{w}_{\text{gen}},a_{\texttt{IDM}})</annotation></semantics></math>, we form the video pair <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathbf{w}_{\text{gen}},\mathbf{w}_{\text{sim}}(a_{\texttt{IDM}}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mtext>gen</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mtext>sim</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">IDM</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathbf{w}_{\text{gen}},\mathbf{w}_{\text{sim}}(a_{\texttt{IDM}}))</annotation></semantics></math> and feed it to the trained attentive probe <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>. We retain the sample only if the alignment probability <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> exceeds a threshold <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>, indicating the two videos are motion-consistent. Further details are provided in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS3" title="A.3 Attentive Probe Training ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Improve Neural Trajectory via Best-of-N Sampling</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our filtering method can be used not only to select beneficial synthetic data but also to improve the neural trajectory by serving as a critic for the video generative model at inference time. Concretely, we adopt a Best-of-N sampling strategy: (1) we sample <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> candidate videos along with their IDM-predicted actions, and (2) we select the video-action pair with the highest critic score. As the critic score, we use the alignment probability <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> introduced in Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Action-level Filtering of Neural Trajectory ‣ 3 Method ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>, which measures whether the motion in the synthetic video is consistent with the simulator rollout. A higher score indicates better alignment between the generated video and the IDM-inferred actions, making the selected pair more suitable for policy learning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This strategy is particularly appealing in fine-tuning settings, where data collection is typically constrained to a specific target task. Importantly, Best-of-N sampling improves the quality of neural trajectory without discarding samples, enabling more effective use of our neural trajectory generation framework in data-scarce settings.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18742v1/experiment_overview.svg" id="S3.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:381/336;" width="381" height="336"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S3.F4.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
<span id="S3.F4.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">An overview of experimental design for RoboCurate.</span>
We conduct two-phase experiments: (1) pre-training on real data and neural trajectory followed by fine-tuning on simulation data, and (2) co-finetuning on real data and neural trajectory.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S4.T1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Performance comparison on GR-1 Tabletop <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">NVIDIA et al., 2025</a>)</cite><span id="S4.T1.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">. We report the average success rate (%) over 50 trials across 24 tasks (18 rearrangement and 6 articulated), trained with varying number of demonstrations. DreamGen <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> denotes neural trajectory generated by I2V model and labeled with IDM-predicted actions, without our visual diversity pipeline. For a fair comparison, all methods that leverage synthetic data use the same pre-filtering dataset size of 10K neural trajectory.</span></span></figcaption>

<figure id="S4.T2" class="ltx_table ltx_figure_panel">
<br class="ltx_break ltx_break">
<table id="S4.T2.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S4.T2.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T2.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt">Method</td>
<td id="S4.T2.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt">Synth.</td>
<td id="S4.T2.1.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt">Filtering</td>
<td id="S4.T2.1.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt">GR-1 Humanoid</td>
<td id="S4.T2.1.1.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt">Bimanual Panda Arms (Dexterous Hands)</td>
<td id="S4.T2.1.1.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S4.T2.1.1.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Avg.</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T2.1.2" class="ltx_tr">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T2.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 2</span>: </span><span id="S4.T2.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Performance comparison on DexMimicGen <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2025</a>)</cite><span id="S4.T2.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">. We report the average success rate (%) over 50 trials across 6 tasks (3 GR-1 Humanoid and 3 Bimanual Panda Arms (Dexterous Hands)), trained with 100 demonstrations per task. Results for tables are averaged over 3 random seeds. DreamGen <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> denotes neural trajectory generated by I2V model and labeled with IDM-predicted actions, without our visual diversity pipeline. For a fair comparison, all methods that leverage synthetic data use the same pre-filtering dataset size of 10K neural trajectory.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We design experiments to answer the following research questions:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Does data generated by RoboCurate effectively improve vision-language-action models (VLAs) when applied in the pre-training stage (see Tables <a href="#S4" title="4 Experiments ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and <a href="#S4" title="4 Experiments ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>)?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Does data generated by RoboCurate effectively improve VLAs when applied in the co-finetuning stage (see Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Datasets. ‣ 4.1 Pre-training Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>)?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">How effective is the diversity augmentation strategy in RoboCurate (see Tables <a href="#S4" title="4 Experiments ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, <a href="#S4" title="4 Experiments ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, and <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ Baselines. ‣ 4.2 Co-finetuning Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>)?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">How effective is the filtering strategy proposed in RoboCurate (see Tables <a href="#S4" title="4 Experiments ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, <a href="#S4" title="4 Experiments ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 4.2 Co-finetuning Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, and  <a href="#S4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ Baselines. ‣ 4.2 Co-finetuning Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>)?</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate RoboCurate and answer these questions under two training regimes: (1) two-stage training: pre-training followed by fine-tuning, and (2) co-finetuning on real data and neural trajectory. We provide a brief overview of our experimental design in Figure <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Improve Neural Trajectory via Best-of-N Sampling ‣ 3 Method ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.</p>
</div>

</span></figcaption>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Pre-training Experiments</h3>

<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Datasets.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For the pre-training stage, we use ActionNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fourier ActionNet Team, 2025</a>)</cite> as the default pre-training dataset. ActionNet consists of bimanual tabletop manipulation trajectories collected on Fourier GR1-T1 humanoid, captured from an ego-view camera. GR1-T1 humanoid is equipped with 6-DoF dexterous hands, resulting in a total of 44-dimensional joint-space states and actions. While the original dataset has 30K teleoperated episodes, we use a 3K subset for pre-training by applying unique prompt filtering to reduce redundant episodes with identical task instructions. We use this dataset for both video generative model training and policy learning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For the fine-tuning stage, we fine-tune and evaluate models on two simulated dexterous manipulation benchmarks: GR-1 Tabletop <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">NVIDIA et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and DexMimicGen <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. GR-1 Tabletop focuses on dexterous hand control for tabletop manipulation and includes a variety of objects and placements. DexMimicGen focuses on bimanual manipulation and supports cross-embodiment evaluation, such as Panda arms and GR-1 humanoid.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 3</span>: </span><span id="S4.T3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Performance comparison on ALLEX humanoid.<span id="S4.T3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> We report the average success rate (%) over 24 trials across 3 tasks (1 seen task and 2 unseen tasks). We collect 48 demonstrations only for the seen task. We generate synthetic data for both seen and unseen tasks (48 episodes for the seen task and 50 episodes for each unseen task) and co-finetune with real data. DreamGen <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> denotes neural trajectory generated by I2V model and labeled with IDM-predicted actions, without our visual diversity pipeline. * denotes that our filtering strategy is applied during the generation stage via Best-of-N sampling, and visual augmentation is not used in this case.</span></span></figcaption>
