<td id="S4.T3.6.5.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S4.T3.6.5.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-bg-color:#E6FFFF;">43.8</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.6.5.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S4.T3.6.5.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-bg-color:#E6FFFF;">25.0</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.6.5.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S4.T3.6.5.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-bg-color:#E6FFFF;">38.9</span></td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Baselines.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We primarily use GR00T N1.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bjorck et al., 2025</a>)</cite> as the base policy and do not load pre-trained weights for the action head. We design our baselines along two axes: (1) the choice of pre-training data, and (2) whether action-level filtering is applied. For pre-training data, we consider three settings: (1) real data only, (2) real data combined with neural trajectory following the pipeline of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al. (2025)</a></cite>, and (3) real data combined with our visually augmented neural trajectory via I2I and V2V pipeline. In particular, the neural trajectory in (2) consists of image-to-video generation and pseudo-action labeling by IDM, without our visual diversity strategy. We further compare uncurated and curated versions of visually augmented neural trajectory in (3) to evaluate the effect of our filtering strategy. We provide full implementation details for policy training in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS1" title="A.1 Pre-training Experiments ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a>. We also provide details on neural trajectory generation in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Neural Trajectory Generation ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Experimental results.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4" title="4 Experiments ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and <a href="#S4" title="4 Experiments ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> show that pre-training with our synthetic data generation framework consistently outperforms all other baselines. First, we observe that our visual augmentation pipeline (e.g., I2I editing and V2V transfer) substantially improves downstream task performance. Second, our action-level filtering is effective for curating neural trajectory and further enhances VLA performance, even with a smaller amount of data. Finally, the effectiveness of our neural trajectory is not limited to a single embodiment; neural trajectory’s prior can be transferred across embodiments, <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e</span>.<span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">g</span>., a policy pre-trained with GR-1 humanoid neural trajectory can be successfully fine-tuned for bimanual Panda arms with dexterous hands.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Co-finetuning Experiments</h3>

<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Datasets.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We design real-world tasks with Allex humanoid to validate that neural trajectory can improve real-world generalization without collecting additional real data. Allex humanoid is equipped with an ego-view camera and two 15-DoF dexterous hands, yielding 48-dimensional joint-space states and actions. Specifically, we conduct experiments on 3 tabletop manipulation tasks: (1) pick-and-place cube, an in-distribution (ID) task for which we manually collect 48 teleoperated demonstrations; (2) pick-and-place cup, an out-of-distribution (OOD) task involving a novel object; and (3) pour can, an OOD task involving a novel behavior. We note that we do not collect any real data for these OOD tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Baselines.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We primarily use a pre-trained GR00T N1.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bjorck et al., 2025</a>)</cite> as the base policy and fine-tune it for ALLEX humanoid. We design baselines to validate that our filtering strategy can directly improve the quality of neural trajectory. For co-finetuning data, we consider three settings: (1) real data only, (2) real data combined with neural trajectory following the pipeline of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al. (2025)</a></cite>, and (3) real data combined with Best-of-N sampled neural trajectory selected by our filtering strategy. Since the co-finetuning phase requires task-specific data, we generate neural trajectory using the same fixed task instruction for each task, following the pipeline in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Neural Trajectory Generation ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>. For Best-of-N sampling in (3), we sample <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> candidates with different random seeds for Gaussian noise, compute the filtering score (see Section <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Improve Neural Trajectory via Best-of-N Sampling ‣ 3 Method ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>), and keep the highest-scoring one; in (2), we generate a single sample using a fixed seed. We provide full implementation details for policy training in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS2" title="A.2 Co-finetuning Experiments ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T5" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 5</span>: </span><span id="S4.T5.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Diversity analysis of RoboCurate on GR-1 Tabletop <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">NVIDIA et al., 2025</a>)</cite><span id="S4.T5.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">. We report the average success rate (%) over 50 trials across 24 tasks (18 rearrangement and 6 articulated), trained with 300 demonstrations per task. For a fair comparison, we fix the dataset size to 10K neural trajectory across all diversity setups.</span></span></figcaption>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 6</span>: </span><span id="S4.T6.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Component-wise ablation of RoboCurate’s filtering strategy on GR-1 Tabletop <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">NVIDIA et al., 2025</a>)</cite><span id="S4.T6.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">. </figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Experimental results.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Datasets. ‣ 4.1 Pre-training Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows that RoboCurate remains effective when co-finetuning policies on real data combined with neural trajectory. Notably, even in the absence of real-world data for out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks (<span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e</span>.<span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">g</span>., pour can), policies trained solely on neural trajectory can successfully perform OOD behaviors (0% <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> 12.5% on pour can). We note that we generate 48 episodes for ID task and 50 episodes for each OOD task in our experiments. Our action-level filtering is applied during video generation, where it serves as a critic in a Best-of-N sampling procedure (see Section <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Improve Neural Trajectory via Best-of-N Sampling ‣ 3 Method ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>). By selecting action-verified video candidates, this strategy yields an additional <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>40% relative gain over using unfiltered neural trajectory. Overall, these results indicate that our action-quality metric can effectively identify beneficial samples for policy learning, leading to improved downstream task performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Ablation Studies and Analyses</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We investigate the effectiveness of the proposed components of RoboCurate under the two-stage training setup shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Improve Neural Trajectory via Best-of-N Sampling ‣ 3 Method ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. We use ActionNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fourier ActionNet Team, 2025</a>)</cite> as the default pre-training dataset and GR00T N1.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bjorck et al., 2025</a>)</cite> as the base policy, without loading pre-trained weights for the action head. Across all ablation experiments, we fix the pre-filtering dataset size to 10K neural trajectory for pre-training. Unless otherwise stated, we follow the same neural trajectory generation pipeline and policy training setup as in the main experiments.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Comparison with other filtering strategies.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To verify the effectiveness of our filtering strategy, we conduct experiments comparing our method with other methods that assess the physical plausibility of generated videos. Table <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 4.2 Co-finetuning Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows that our action-level filtering outperforms video-only physical plausibility filtering methods. In particular, DreamGenBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> queries VLM with a fixed prompt to judge whether a generated video violates basic physics. Similarly, VideoCon-Physics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bansal et al., 2024</a>)</cite> queries VideoCon, a 7B VLM, to predict whether a video follows physical laws. Our results demonstrate that verifying action quality is crucial for policy learning, whereas relying solely on VLM-based video-level plausibility assessments is insufficient for curating beneficial synthetic data.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F6" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18742v1/main_benchmark_singleplot_group_spaced_robocurate_bold_legend14_axis14.svg" id="S4.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/283;" width="452" height="283"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="S4.F6.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
<span id="S4.F6.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Aggregation of RoboCurate performance.</span> Comparison of VLA performance across different pre-training or co-finetuning settings on GR-1 Tabletop <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">NVIDIA et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, DexMimicGen <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and real-world benchmark. RoboCurate shows strong performance across all settings.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Effect of attentive-probe training.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To better understand the mechanism for identifying visual motion consistency, we conduct a component-wise ablation of the action verifier. Table <a href="#S4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ Baselines. ‣ 4.2 Co-finetuning Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> shows that the attentive probe trained on V-JEPA2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Assran et al., 2025</a>)</cite> features using our proposed strategy yields the best VLA performance, outperforming other baselines. As a simple baseline, we filter samples by thresholding the cosine similarity between frozen video encoder embeddings of a generated video and its simulator replay. However, this similarity-based filter yields limited gains, as the pre-trained encoder may not generalize well to simulator rollouts and instead rely on appearance cues rather than motion. In contrast, our probe learns a motion-consistency classifier on fused video embeddings, enabling the detection of subtle motion discrepancies between a generated video and its simulator replay. Moreover, obtaining reliable supervision is non-trivial: human labels provide little benefit and can even underperform the naive baseline, likely due to noisy judgments on subtle action mismatches. By contrast, our automatic positive/negative pair construction (see Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ Expanding visual diversity. ‣ 3.1 Generating Plausible Manipulation Scenarios ‣ 3 Method ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>) offers consistent supervision for fine-grained motion differences, leading to improved downstream performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Effect of diversity in neural trajectory.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate the effect of diversity in our neural trajectory, we analyze two factors: (1) task diversity and (2) visual diversity. Table <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ Baselines. ‣ 4.2 Co-finetuning Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> indicates that VLA performance increases monotonically with higher task diversity under a fixed dataset size of 10K neural trajectory. Specifically, we vary task diversity by changing the number of distinct tasks, where each task corresponds to a unique combination of skill, target object, placement, and hand type (<span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i</span>.<span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e</span>., combinatorial coverage). These results highlight the importance of carefully designing prompts for VLM to generate diverse task instructions. Moreover, Table <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ Baselines. ‣ 4.2 Co-finetuning Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> demonstrates that RoboCurate’s visual diversity pipeline further improves performance while keeping the same task diversity ratio, underscoring the value of visually diverse observations beyond task coverage alone.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Video generative models for robot learning.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Video generative models were originally developed for general human video generation, and prior work has explored using such videos to provide novel scenes or motions for robot policy learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bharadhwaj et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, sometimes combined with simple tracking signals <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Another line of work leverages text-to-video (T2V) diffusion models to generate synthetic trajectories and infer pseudo actions via inverse dynamics models (IDMs) for task generalization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Luo et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. More recent studies further explore using video generative models as the robot policy itself, treating video prediction as a proxy for policy learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Alongside these trends, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al. (2025)</a></cite> adopt state-of-the-art video generative models as a data generation pipeline that synthesizes robot videos and extracts pseudo actions for policy training. Our method also follows this data-centric pipeline, using video generation as a source of synthetic experience for learning from limited robot data.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Synthetic data generation for robot policies.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Collecting large-scale real-world robot data is costly and labor-intensive, which has led many works to rely on simulation datasets as a primary alternative <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mandlekar et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nasiriany et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. While simulation enables scalable data collection, it suffers from several limitations, including the sim-to-real gap, inaccurate physical modeling, and difficulties in handling articulated objects, deformable materials, or complex tool interactions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. As an alternative, recent works explore generating synthetic robot data using generative models, aiming to bypass simulation constraints and improve scalability <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mandi et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Alhaija et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. However, such approaches often suffer from limited visual and scene diversity. For example, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al. (2025)</a></cite> first samples plausible task instructions from an initial image, and then generates synthetic robot videos using image-to-video (I2V) models, but diversity remains constrained by the manually collected initial visual context. In contrast, our method explicitly increases visual diversity by combining image-to-image (I2I) editing and video-to-video (V2V) transfer, enabling broader variation in scenes and appearances for synthetic data generation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present RoboCurate, a synthetic robot data generation framework that improves neural trajectory by (i) verifying IDM-predicted actions through simulator-replay consistency and (ii) expanding observation diversity via I2I editing and action-preserving V2V transfer. Our results show that increasing the visual diversity of neural trajectory is a key driver of downstream policy performance, and that our I2I and V2V pipeline yields more beneficial synthetic data than naive I2V generation. Moreover, our action-consistency measure is effective both for filtering training data for policy learning and as a critic for Best-of-N sampling in video generation, consistently boosting performance across simulation and real-world benchmarks. We hope RoboCurate encourages principled quality evaluation for synthetic robot data and enables more effective policy learning from curated neural trajectory.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Impact Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This paper presents RoboCurate , a framework to expand the capabilities of robot policies using synthetic robot data. The framework suggests that a policy can learn novel actions present in synthetic robot data. Careful consideration is required to ensure that synthetic robot data and resulting policies align with social values.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Implementation Details</h2>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Pre-training Experiments</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For the pre-training stage, we adopt Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD; <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>) learning rate scheduler for policy training. Specifically, we pre-train all models for 60K gradient steps, maintaining a constant high learning rate for the first 50K steps, followed by a sharp decay over the last 10K steps. We hypothesize that the quality of neural trajectory becomes more critical after the model has observed a sufficient amount of data. Therefore, we use all neural trajectory for the first 50K steps and switch to only curated neural trajectory (by RoboCurate) after 50K steps. Second, we use separate embodiment tags for real (from ActionNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fourier ActionNet Team, 2025</a>)</cite>) and neural trajectory, even though they share the same GR-1 embodiment, since the statistics of IDM actions differ from those of ActionNet. During training, we sample real and neural trajectory in a 1:1 ratio by default. Otherwise, we follow the original training configuration of GR00T N1.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bjorck et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, except that we set the global batch size to 512  and train for 60K global steps.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For the fine-tuning stage, we fine-tune GR00T N1.5 from the pre-trained checkpoint corresponding to each experimental setup (see Section <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Pre-training Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>). We note that the fine-tuning dataset is identical for the same fine-tuning task. We follow the original GR00T N1.5 fine-tuning configurations, except that we set the global batch size to 256 and tune the number of gradient steps per downstream task dataset (up to 60K gradient steps) to optimize performance. We train separate models for different embodiments and observation viewpoints (<span id="A1.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e</span>.<span id="A1.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">g</span>., GR-1 humanoid in ego view, GR-1 humanoid in front view, and bimanual Panda arms with dexterous hands) on DexMimicGen <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Co-finetuning Experiments</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We follow the training setup of GR00T N1.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bjorck et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and fine-tune a pretrained GR00T N1.5 model for 10K gradient steps. During co-finetuning, we mix real and neural data and maintain a 1:1:1 sampling ratio across ”Pick and place can”, ”Pick and place cup”, and ”Pour can” tasks. We follow the original GR00T N1.5 fine-tuning configurations, except that we set the global batch size to 128 and the number of gradient steps to 10K.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>Attentive Probe Training</h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We train an attentive probe on top of V-JEPA2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Assran et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. We follow the V-JEPA2 implementation and training strategy, and attach the probe to a pre-trained 0.3B V-JEPA2 large model wtih the backbone frozen during training. The hyperparameters for attentive probe training are as follows.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.T7" class="ltx_table">

<tr id="A1.T7.5.10" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A1.T7.5.10.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb"><span id="A1.T7.5.10.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Maximum epochs</span></td>
<td id="A1.T7.5.10.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="A1.T7.5.10.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">50</span></td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Neural Trajectory Generation</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Video generation.</span> We use Cosmos-Predict2-14B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nvidia, 2026</a>)</cite> as the base video generative model and fine-tune it from the pre-trained checkpoint. Specifically, we fine-tune on ActionNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fourier ActionNet Team, 2025</a>)</cite> and GR00T-GR1-100<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          <a href="https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/PhysicalAI-Robotics-GR00T-GR1" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/PhysicalAI-Robotics-GR00T-GR1</a></span></span></span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> for the pre-training experiments, and on a manually collected ALLEX dataset for the co-finetuning experiments. Unless otherwise stated, we generate approximately 10K tabletop manipulation videos. For the co-finetuning setup, we instead generate 48/50/50 videos per one ID task and two OOD tasks, respectively. All videos are conditioned on initial images from the fine-tuning datasets and plausible task instructions. We use Gemini 3 Pro <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Google, 2025</a>)</cite> to generate instructions for each initial image using a carefully designed system prompt. We provide more details in Appendix <a href="#A3.SS1" title="C.1 Task Instruction for Image-to-Video Generative Model ‣ Appendix C Prompt for VLM ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In addition, we use FLUX.2-dev <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Labs, 2025</a>)</cite> for image editing and Cosmos-Transfer2.5-2B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ali et al., 2025</a>)</cite> for video-to-video transfer as visual augmentation (see Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Generating Plausible Manipulation Scenarios ‣ 3 Method ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>), except in the co-finetuning experiments. For image editing, we use initial images from the same dataset used for video generation, and for V2V transfer, we use the subset of previously generated videos as input. We note that we generate approximately 10K augmented tabletop manipulation videos, with an I2I:V2V ratio of 2:1 for efficiency given the generation cost.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Post-processing.</span> We apply post-processing to our neural trajectory along two axes, inspired by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">NVIDIA et al. (2025)</a></cite>: (1) instruction following and (2) trajectory plausibility. First, we filter out videos conditioned on implausible tasks, as the initial instructions generated by VLM may be ill-posed. Second, we check whether the generated videos correctly follow instructions, and re-caption videos that do not follow the instructions. Since instruction following directly determines task success, we apply this post-processing to all neural trajectory dataset by default (resulting in exactly 10K neural trajectory after this step, except in the co-finetuning stage). Finally, we check whether robot hand trajectories in the generated videos are plausible, exhibiting correct sense of depth and spatial orientation. We focus on this aspect due to common failures in neural trajectory involving incorrect approach distances and object interactions. We prompt VLM to evaluate the video on a Likert scale from 1 to 5 and select videos with score greater than or equal to 3. We use Gemini 3 Pro <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Google, 2025</a>)</cite> for instruction following post-processing and Gemini 2.5 Flash <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Comanici et al., 2025</a>)</cite> for trajectory plausibility post-processing, by feeding 8 video frames as input. Details of the specific prompts used are provided in Appendix <a href="#A3.SS2" title="C.2 Post-processing for Neural Trajectory ‣ Appendix C Prompt for VLM ‣ RoboCurate: Harnessing Diversity with Action-Verified Neural Trajectory for Robot Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.2</span></a>. We note that trajectory plausibility post-processing is applied only prior to out action-level filtering stage.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pseudo-action labeling.</span> We use diffusion transformer with SigLIP-2 vision encoder <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tschannen et al., 2025</a>)</cite> as our base IDM, following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al. (2025)</a></cite>. For pre-training setup, we use an open-source pre-trained checkpoint<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          <a href="https://huggingface.co/seonghyeonye/IDM_gr1" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://huggingface.co/seonghyeonye/IDM_gr1</a></span></span></span> for GR-1 embodiment. For fine-tuning setup, we train the IDM from scratch for ALLEX embodiment using manually collected data (the same data used to fine-tune the video model), with a global batch size of 64, and 20K gradient steps.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">

</span><span id="lstnumberx15.22" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">task</span>.<span id="lstnumberx15.23" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx15.24" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">Use</span><span id="lstnumberx15.25" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx15.26" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">the</span><span id="lstnumberx15.27" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>[<span id="lstnumberx15.28" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">specified</span><span id="lstnumberx15.29" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span     <h2>Instructions for reporting errors</h2>
    <p>We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile
      support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the
      methods listed below:</p>
    <ul>
      <li>Click the "Report Issue" <span class="mobile-only">(<svg role="presentation"
            style="display: inline-block; vertical-align: middle; fill: var(--text-color);" aria-hidden="true"

    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>

        href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.</p>
